key_terms.meaning: One-chip computer: CPU, flash, RAM, EEPROM, ADC, timers, PWM, CAN; reads sensors and drives outputs in real time.
P = I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub>; a 4.07 A lamp through 10 mΩ loses 0.166 W.
A device that converts a physical quantity (temperature, pressure, speed) into an electrical signal the ECU can read.
The circuit block that amplifies, filters and scales a raw sensor output into the 0–5 V range an ADC can accept.
Analog-to-digital converter: count = round(V × (2<sup>n</sup> − 1) ÷ V<sub>ref</sub>); a 10-bit ADC on 5 V resolves 5 ÷ 1023 = 4.89 mV.
Active sensors need an excitation supply (potentiometer, Hall IC); passive sensors generate their own signal (thermocouple, piezoelectric knock sensor).
Absolute pressure is measured against vacuum; relative (gauge) pressure is measured against ambient, so absolute = gauge + atmospheric.
A correction added to a thermocouple reading, because the thermocouple measures the difference between the hot junction and the cooler reference junction.
ṁ = η<sub>v</sub> p V<sub>d</sub> (N ÷ 2) ÷ (R T), N in rev/s; 60 kPa, 300 K, 1.6 L, 3000 rpm, η<sub>v</sub> 0.90 gives 25.1 g/s.
A heated wire in the intake stream is held at constant temperature; the current needed to keep it hot rises with air mass flow and becomes the flow signal.
Manifold absolute pressure sensor; a silicon diaphragm with piezoresistive strain gauges gives a voltage proportional to absolute intake pressure.
A gap in the crankshaft target wheel that produces a unique pulse so the ECU can identify top dead centre of cylinder one.
A coil and magnet facing a toothed wheel; each tooth passage generates an AC pulse whose amplitude and frequency rise with speed.
A current-carrying semiconductor in a magnetic field develops a small transverse voltage; a Hall IC switches cleanly when a shutter or magnet passes.
An LED and phototransistor pair with a slotted disc between them; each slot gives a digital pulse, and a wider index slot marks the reference.
Negative temperature coefficient resistor: resistance falls steeply and non-linearly as temperature rises, used for coolant, intake air and cabin air.
The chemically correct air-fuel mass ratio; about 14.7 kg of air per kg of petrol, giving lambda = 1.
A solid-electrolyte cell that produces a voltage when oxygen on its two sides differs; output is a switch around lambda = 1 for the narrowband type.
A ceramic disc bolted to the block that produces a charge when the block vibrates, letting the ECU detect detonation and retard spark.
A solenoid converts coil current into a straight pull; a stepper motor turns in fixed angular steps as its coils are energised in sequence.
F = Δp × A, v = Q ÷ A, P = Δp × Q; a 60 mm wastegate diaphragm opens against 90 N at 31.8 kPa.
E = kΦω, V = E + I R<sub>a</sub>, T = kΦ I; speed falls in a straight line with torque to stall at V ÷ R<sub>a</sub>.
IEC 60034-1 S1 to S10; S1 continuous, S2 short-time, S3 intermittent with CDF = t<sub>on</sub> ÷ (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>).
n<sub>s</sub> = 120 f ÷ p; an induction machine runs at n<sub>s</sub>(1 − s).
Battery state of charge is estimated by integrating measured current over time; SOC is the remaining charge as a fraction of rated capacity.

takeaways: Every sensor and actuator meets a microcontroller: its ADC, capture timers and PWM outputs set how finely and how fast the ECU can measure and act.
Automotive electronics must survive −40 °C to 125 °C and more, a sagging and spiky supply, vibration and interference; MOSFET drivers and smart switches are built for this.
Signal conditioning (bridge, amplifier, filter, divider) and the ADC decide the resolution you can use; one 10-bit count on 5 V is 4.89 mV.
Air charge is measured directly by a mass air flow meter or estimated from MAP by speed density; the choice changes the fuel calculation.
Crankshaft sensing gives both angle and speed; the missing-tooth gap (3T on a 60-2 wheel) fixes the reference.
Hall and optical sensors give a signal down to zero speed; a variable-reluctance sensor gives an AC voltage that grows with speed and vanishes at standstill.
The oxygen sensor closes the fuel loop: it measures the result of combustion, and the ECU trims injection from it.
Knock, acceleration and rate sensors work on vibration and motion and feed protection and stability functions, not fuel metering.
Electromechanical actuators (solenoids, relays, steppers) are switched coils; fluid-mechanical actuators let a small valve command a large force, F = Δp × A.
Electric motors are chosen by type (DC, brushless, three-phase) and by duty type; battery current and voltage sensing turn the battery into SOC, SOH and SOF.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for a labelled block diagram: the ECU with its microcontroller, or the sensor, its conditioning circuit and the ECU input. Long answers should then explain how a wrong signal changes fuel, spark or actuator action, and work any numbers to a final value with units.

bank.q: Explain the demands placed on automotive electronics. Describe the semiconductor components used in an engine ECU and, with a block diagram, the microcontroller and how it processes data.
outline: Demands: temperature, supply and transients, vibration, EMC, life, safety, cost
Semiconductors: doping, pn junction, forward voltage
Components: diodes (rectifier, freewheeling, Zener/TVS), BJT, MOSFET, IGBT, ICs and smart switches
MCU blocks: CPU, flash, RAM, EEPROM, ADC, capture timer, PWM, CAN, watchdog
Data processing: read, check plausibility, map with interpolation, drive outputs, log faults; interrupts for crank teeth
answer: Demands. An ECU must work from −40 °C to 125 °C or more near the engine, on a 12 V supply that varies between about 9 V and 16 V, sags while cranking and carries spikes and load-dump transients; it must survive vibration, humidity and salt, meet electromagnetic compatibility (neither emit nor suffer interference), last 15 years or more, check itself where safety depends on it, and be cheap in millions.

Semiconductor basics. Silicon is doped with phosphorus (n-type, free electrons) or boron (p-type, holes). Where they meet a pn junction forms: it conducts forward above about 0.6 to 0.7 V and blocks reverse current. Diodes, transistors and integrated circuits are built from junctions.

head: Component
Job in the ECU
rows: Path for coil current at switch-off
Clamps spikes on supply and sensor lines
Injector, lamp, valve and motor drivers; loss I² R<sub>DS(on)</sub>
Microcontroller, voltage regulator, CAN transceiver, smart high-side switch

answer.text: Block diagram of the ECU and its microcontroller:
answer.pre:
sensors → input filter/protection → [ADC | capture timer]
                                   ↓
          [CPU] ↔ [flash: program, maps] [RAM] [EEPROM]
                                   ↓
          [PWM / compare outputs] → MOSFET drivers → injectors, coils, valves
          [CAN / LIN] ↔ other ECUs        [watchdog] resets the MCU if the program stalls

answer: Each block: the CPU executes the program; flash keeps the program and calibration maps; RAM holds working values; EEPROM keeps learnt values and fault codes after switch-off; the ADC converts sensor voltages (10 or 12 bits); capture timers time-stamp crank-tooth edges; compare and PWM outputs fire injectors and coils at set angles; CAN and LIN carry data to other ECUs; the watchdog resets a stalled program.

Data processing: the program reads the inputs, checks each for plausibility (range, rate of change, agreement of redundant sensors), looks up maps over speed and load with linear interpolation, computes injection time and spark angle, drives the outputs and stores fault codes. Fast events (crank teeth) arrive as interrupts; slow ones (coolant) are read every 10 to 100 ms.
Interpolation example: a map holds 20° at 2000 rpm and 26° at 3000 rpm, so at 2500 rpm the ECU uses 20 + 6 × 500 ÷ 1000 = 23°.

Timing check: at 6000 rpm a 60-2 wheel gives a tooth every 1 ÷ (100 × 60) s = 166.7 µs, which is 13 333 clock cycles of an 80 MHz MCU; a 1500-cycle tooth routine uses 11 % of the CPU, leaving time for the other tasks.

Why MOSFETs drive the outputs: for a 55 W lamp (4.07 A at 13.5 V) a 10 mΩ MOSFET loses 4.07² × 0.010 = 0.166 W and needs almost no gate current, while a bipolar transistor would lose 0.3 × 4.07 = 1.22 W and need 0.204 A of base current, far more than a microcontroller pin can give.

bank.q: Define a sensor and classify automotive sensors by the quantity measured, by active or passive nature, and by contact or non-contact operation. Explain the signal conditioning chain from sensor to ADC.
outline: Definition: physical quantity to electrical signal
Classification: position, speed, pressure, flow, temperature, gas concentration, torque, vibration
Active needs excitation; passive self-generating
Contact wears; non-contact (Hall, optical, inductive) does not
Conditioning: protection, excitation, bridge, amplify, filter (low-pass anti-alias), scale to ADC range
ADC resolution example: 10-bit on 5 V reference gives about 4.9 mV per step
answer: Definition: a sensor converts a physical quantity (temperature, pressure, position, speed, gas concentration) into an electrical signal the ECU can read. The transducer is the element that does the conversion.

head: Quantity
Sensor
rows: Hot wire or film, Karman vortex

answer: Active and passive: in the automotive convention an active sensor needs an excitation supply (thermistor, potentiometer, Hall IC) and a passive one generates its own signal (thermocouple, piezo knock sensor, reluctance coil). Many instrumentation books use the opposite words, so name the convention in the answer.

Contact and non-contact: a potentiometer wiper rubs and wears; Hall, optical and inductive sensors read a target across an air gap and do not wear. Analog sensors give a continuous voltage; digital ones a pulse train or code.

answer.text: The conditioning chain from sensor to ADC:
answer.pre: sensing element → excitation / bridge → amplifier → low-pass filter → (linearise) → sample and hold → ADC → ECU

answer: Each stage: protection clamps spikes; excitation (a stable 5 V) and a Wheatstone bridge turn a small resistance change into a differential voltage; an instrumentation amplifier scales it to the ADC window; a low-pass filter (corner f = 1 ÷ 2πRC) removes ignition noise and prevents aliasing; a table or polynomial linearises; the sample-and-hold freezes the value while the ADC converts.
ADC resolution: count = round(V × (2<sup>n</sup> − 1) ÷ V<sub>ref</sub>). A 10-bit ADC on 5 V resolves 5 ÷ 1023 = 4.89 mV, about the 4.9 mV of the outline.

Worked figure: the coolant divider (1 kΩ to 5 V, NTC to ground) gives 5 × 2000 ÷ 3000 = 3.333 V (count 682) at 25 °C and 5 × 500 ÷ 1500 = 1.667 V (count 341) at 80 °C. The count is a voltage code, not a temperature: the ECU maps it through the sensor table.
Specification words to quote: range, span, sensitivity (with units), resolution, accuracy, linearity, hysteresis, drift and response time.
Closing check: a good answer names the sensor, its principle, its output type and its conditioning stage for at least four quantities, and shows one number worked through the chain to an ADC count.

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a hot-wire mass air flow sensor and a piezoresistive MAP sensor. State the advantages and limits of each.
outline: Hot wire: heated element in intake, constant-temperature bridge, current is the flow signal
Hot film and compensation element for air temperature
Needs burn-off cycle after shut-down to clean the wire
MAP: silicon diaphragm, diffused piezoresistive gauges, Wheatstone bridge, absolute pressure
MAP used in speed-density fuel calculation with engine speed and intake air temperature
Limits: MAF sensitive to dirt and backflow pulsation; MAP needs a barometric reference for altitude
answer: Hot-wire construction: a thin platinum wire (or a film on a ceramic chip in the hot-film type) sits in the intake air stream with a second, unheated element that measures air temperature. Both are arms of a Wheatstone bridge.

Working: the bridge amplifier drives just enough current through the heated element to keep it a fixed temperature above the air. More air mass carries away more heat, so more current is needed; the bridge current (as a voltage across a measuring resistor) is the mass-flow signal. Because heat transfer depends on mass, not volume, no density correction is needed.
Burn-off: after the engine stops, the ECU heats the wire to about 1000 °C for about a second to burn off deposits that would change its heat transfer and calibration.

Advantages: direct mass flow, fast response, no moving parts, low pressure loss, automatic altitude compensation. Limits: dirt and oil on the element shift calibration; pulsating and reverse flow at low speed and wide throttle can be over-read unless the sensor detects flow direction; leaks after the meter are not measured.

MAP construction: a silicon diaphragm with a sealed vacuum on one side and manifold pressure on the other; four piezoresistive resistors diffused into it form a Wheatstone bridge, and the amplifier and temperature compensation are on the same chip.

Working: manifold pressure bends the diaphragm, the strained resistors change value, and the bridge gives a voltage proportional to absolute pressure, for example V = 0.05 p − 0.5 (0.5 V at 20 kPa to 4.5 V at 100 kPa); 60 kPa reads 2.5 V.

answer.text: Speed-density use, with the chapter's numbers (1.6 L, 3000 rpm, 60 kPa, 300 K, η<sub>v</sub> = 0.90):

answer: MAP advantages: cheap, robust, quick to respond to throttle changes, also gives barometric pressure at key-on. Limits: depends on a stored volumetric-efficiency table and on correct intake temperature; it cannot see engine wear or cam changes, and needs the barometric reading for altitude.
Comparison: MAF measures what enters; MAP infers it. Many ECUs use MAF for steady running and MAP for transients and diagnosis.

bank.q: Explain how the crankshaft angular position and engine speed are sensed, and how the ECU uses the reference mark for ignition and fuel timing.
outline: Target wheel on crank pulley or flywheel, tooth count sets angular resolution
Missing tooth or extra tooth gives a unique reference pulse at a known angle before top dead centre
Speed from pulse frequency, angle from pulse count since reference
Variable reluctance gives an AC signal; Hall gives a square wave
ECU calculates ignition advance and injection start angle from angle and speed
Also drives the tachometer and the stall detection
answer: The target: a steel wheel on the crank pulley or flywheel with teeth on a fixed pitch, for example 60-2 (60 pitches of 6°, two teeth removed) or 36-1 (36 pitches of 10°, one removed). The tooth pitch sets the basic angular resolution; the ECU interpolates between teeth in time.

The sensor: a variable-reluctance (inductive) sensor of magnet and coil gives an AC voltage whose amplitude rises with speed and whose zero crossing marks a tooth centre; a Hall or magnetoresistive sensor gives a square wave of fixed height that works down to zero speed.
Speed: from the time T between normal tooth edges, n = 1 ÷ (z T) rev/s with z the number of pitches. At 3000 rpm on a 60-2 wheel T = 20 ms ÷ 60 = 0.333 ms.

Reference mark: the missing teeth give one interval much longer than the rest, 3T on a 60-2 wheel (1.0 ms at 3000 rpm) and 2T on a 36-1 wheel. The ECU compares each interval with the previous one; a ratio near 3 (or 2) marks the gap. It then resets its tooth counter and gives the next tooth its stored angle, a calibrated number of degrees before top dead centre of cylinder 1.

Phase: a crank wheel turns twice per four-stroke cycle, so the same gap appears at TDC compression and TDC exhaust. The camshaft sensor (one pulse per two crank turns) tells the ECU which, enabling sequential injection and coil-on-plug ignition.

Ignition timing: the ECU looks up the advance (say 26° BTDC) from its speed-load map, counts teeth from the reference to the tooth just before that angle, and sets a timer for the remaining fraction of a pitch, using the latest tooth period to convert angle into time.
Fuel timing: the start of injection is placed the same way at a crank angle before the intake valve opens; the pulse width comes from the air charge.
Other uses: the tachometer, idle-speed control, the rev limiter, misfire detection from tooth-period changes, and stall detection when no tooth arrives within a time-out.
Check of the numbers: on a 60-2 wheel at 3000 rpm, 57 normal intervals of 0.333 ms plus one gap of 1.0 ms make 19.0 + 1.0 = 20.0 ms, exactly one revolution.

bank.q: Describe throttle position sensing with a potentiometer and coolant temperature sensing with an NTC thermistor, including the 5 V reference and voltage divider.
outline: Potentiometer: three wires, 5 V reference, ground, wiper voltage proportional to angle
Two-track potentiometers for plausibility checking
Idle and wide-open-throttle switch contacts in older types
NTC: resistance falls with temperature, non-linear, so the ECU uses a lookup table
Divider formula: V<sub>out</sub> = 5 × R<sub>NTC</sub> ÷ (R<sub>NTC</sub> + R<sub>pull</sub>)
Fail-safe values: throttle default, coolant default for cold start
answer: Throttle potentiometer: three wires (5 V reference, ground, wiper). The track lies across the reference; the wiper, turned by the throttle shaft, picks off a voltage proportional to angle: V = V<sub>0</sub> + k θ.
Numbers: 0.5 V closed and 4.5 V wide open give k = 4.0 ÷ 100 = 0.04 V per %. At 30 % the output is 0.5 + 1.2 = 1.70 V, count round(1.70 × 1023 ÷ 5) = 348.

Plausibility: two tracks with opposite slopes (or a fixed ratio) go to separate ADC channels; the ECU checks each stays within 0.5 to 4.5 V and that their sum or ratio is right. The end bands below 0.5 V and above 4.5 V let it detect a short to ground or to 5 V.

Older types add an idle contact (confirms closed throttle for idle control) and a wide-open-throttle contact (full-load enrichment); these are switches, not angle sensors. Contactless Hall or inductive sensors replace the wiper on modern throttle bodies.
NTC thermistor: a semiconductor ceramic whose resistance falls steeply and non-linearly as temperature rises. It sits from the ECU input to ground with a pull-up resistor to the 5 V reference.

answer.text: Divider and numbers (2.2 kΩ at 25 °C, B = 3500 K, 2.2 kΩ pull-up):

answer: Linearisation: the curve is not straight, so the ECU uses a table of voltage against temperature (or the Steinhart–Hart equation) with more points where fuel correction matters.
Ratiometric reading: the same 5 V feeds the divider and the ADC reference, so slow drift of the 5 V cancels; a bad ground does not cancel.

Fail-safe values: if the TPS is implausible the ECU limits power and uses a limp-home value; if the coolant sensor is open or shorted (voltage near 5 V or 0 V) it uses a default warm-up value and runs the fan.

bank.q: Explain the working of the exhaust gas oxygen sensor and how it closes the fuel loop. Compare narrowband and wideband types.
outline: Zirconia electrolyte conducts oxygen ions above about 300 degrees Celsius
Nernst voltage switches sharply around lambda = 1; heater brings it up to temperature fast
Narrowband: switch output about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich
Wideband: pumping cell with a reference, current proportional to lambda over a wide range
ECU short-term and long-term fuel trim from the sensor signal
Closed loop only after the sensor is hot; open loop at start and full load
answer: Purpose: hold the mixture at λ = 1, where the three-way catalyst converts CO, HC and NO<sub>x</sub> together. λ = AFR<sub>actual</sub> ÷ AFR<sub>stoich</sub>, with 14.7 for petrol.

Construction of the narrowband sensor: a thimble (or planar strip) of yttria-stabilised zirconia, porous platinum electrodes on both faces, exhaust outside, reference air inside, a protective slotted shield and an electric heater.
Working: above about 300 °C zirconia conducts oxygen ions. The oxygen difference across it gives the Nernst voltage E = (RT ÷ 4F) ln(pO₂ ref ÷ pO₂ exh).
So the output switches from about 0.1 V lean to about 0.9 V rich, sharply at λ = 1: it tells the ECU rich or lean, not by how much.

Closing the loop: base fuel comes from the air charge. Short-term trim ramps the injection time down while the sensor reads rich and up while it reads lean, so the mixture oscillates closely about λ = 1; long-term trim learns any steady offset. Example: actual AFR 15.4 gives λ = 15.4 ÷ 14.7 = 1.048, lean, about 0.1 V, so the ECU adds fuel.
Open loop: during warm-up (sensor below light-off) and at full load (deliberately rich) the ECU ignores the sensor; the heater shortens the time to closed loop.

head: Feature
Narrowband
Wideband (UEGO)
rows: Lean burn, diesel, GDI, precise control

answer: Wideband principle: the controller pumps oxygen into or out of a small chamber to hold the Nernst cell at about 450 mV (λ = 1 in the chamber); the pump current needed is proportional to the exhaust's oxygen excess or deficit.

Diagnosis: a healthy narrowband sensor at 2500 rpm switches between about 0.1 V and 0.9 V several times a second; a lazy (poisoned) sensor switches slowly, and one stuck near 0.45 V is usually cold or has an open heater.

bank.q: Describe a piezoelectric knock sensor and an angular-rate sensor, and state how the ECU uses each signal.
outline: Knock: detonation gives block vibration in a characteristic frequency band
Piezoelectric ceramic produces charge proportional to acceleration; charge amplifier converts it
ECU windows the signal after each spark and compares with a threshold
Action: retard spark on the knocking cylinder, then gradually restore advance
Angular rate: vibrating element or MEMS gyroscope giving yaw rate voltage
Used with wheel speed and steering angle for stability control
answer: Knock: self-ignition of the unburnt end gas ahead of the flame front after the spark. The pressure waves ring the cylinder at a frequency set by the bore and gas temperature, typically 5 to 15 kHz, and repeated knock damages pistons and rings.
Construction: a piezoelectric ceramic ring between a seismic mass and the base, bolted to the block with a set torque. Block vibration presses the mass on the ceramic, which produces charge q = d F.

answer.pre:
q = d F = 2 pC/N × 50 N = 100 pC
charge amplifier: V = q ÷ C<sub>f</sub> = 100 pC ÷ 1000 pF = 0.10 V
→ band-pass 5–15 kHz → rectify and integrate → compare with threshold

answer: Crank-angle window: the ECU evaluates the integrated signal only inside a window in the combustion period (about 10° to 60° after TDC of each cylinder), so valve closing and injector noise at other angles are ignored. The threshold is learnt from the background noise of non-knocking cycles.

Action: if a cylinder knocks, the ECU retards its spark by a few degrees at once, then creeps the advance back in small steps; with a turbo it may also lower boost. Running close to the knock limit gives the best efficiency.

Angular-rate sensor: a MEMS structure kept vibrating; when the vehicle yaws, the Coriolis force deflects the vibrating mass at right angles in proportion to the turn rate, and capacitive electrodes read this as a voltage in °/s.

Use: the stability program compares the measured yaw rate with the rate expected from steering angle and speed. If the car turns less than expected (understeer) or more (oversteer), it brakes single wheels and cuts torque to bring the yaw rate back.

Accelerometers complete the set: a lateral accelerometer for the stability program and high-g accelerometers for airbags. In a 50 km/h barrier crash stopping in 80 ms the average deceleration is 13.89 ÷ 0.080 = 173.6 m/s² (17.7 g).
Points of care: a gyro gives rate, not angle; integrating it drifts with bias, so the ECU re-zeros it at standstill.

Checks on the knock sensor: it must be bolted at the specified torque, because the clamp force sets its sensitivity; tapping the block near it with the engine idling should show a burst on an oscilloscope, and an open circuit makes the ECU fall back to a safe, retarded spark map.

bank.q: Explain solenoid, relay and stepper motor actuators in automotive use, with one circuit each for a fuel injector, a relay-driven load and an idle air stepper.
outline: Solenoid: coil pulls plunger, force rises with current, flow area set by pulse width
Injector: peak-and-hold or saturated drive, flyback diode, pulse width sets fuel quantity
Relay: small coil current switches a large load current, coil driven by low-side switch
Stepper: two coils, sequence of steps moves the pintle, no feedback needed, position held by detent
PWM drive for proportional solenoid valves such as EGR and VVT
Failures: open coil, shorted coil, sticking plunger
answer: Solenoid: a coil around a movable iron plunger. Current makes a field that pulls the plunger in; the force F ≈ μ₀N²I²A ÷ (2g²) rises with current squared and falls steeply as the gap g grows.

answer.pre:
+12 V ── injector coil ──┬── drain
                        │  MOSFET (gate ← ECU)
                       ground
(flyback path: diode or active clamp across the coil / switch)

answer: Injector drive: the ECU opens the injector for the pulse width set by the air charge. Peak-and-hold drive gives a high current to open fast, then a low hold current. With N = 500 turns and 1 cm², 1 A gives 15.7 N at a 1 mm gap but 393 N at 0.2 mm, so 0.2 A (10 % PWM on a 6 Ω, 12 V coil) holds it with the same 15.7 N and cuts coil heating from 24 W to 0.24 W.

Relay circuit: the ECU switches a small relay coil (about 100 mA) through a low-side transistor with a freewheeling diode across the coil; the relay contacts carry the heavy load current (fuel pump, fan, horn) from the battery through a fuse.
Why the diode: at switch-off the coil's stored energy ½LI² would otherwise drive its voltage up until the transistor breaks down; the diode lets the current circulate and decay.
Stepper motor: two (or more) phase windings energised in sequence step the rotor by β = 360° ÷ S; a 1.8° motor has 200 steps per revolution, and 400 steps in 0.8 s is 720° (two turns) at 150 rpm.

answer.pre: ECU → two H-bridges → phase A and phase B windings → rotor and lead screw → pintle in the bypass air passage

answer: Idle control: the ECU counts steps from a known end position (it drives against the stop at key-on to reference), so the pintle position is known without a sensor. It is open-loop: overload or too-fast stepping loses steps.
PWM proportional valves: EGR and VVT valves are driven by PWM so the average current, and so the position or pressure, follows the duty cycle.
Failures to name: open or shorted coil (detected by the driver's diagnostics), sticking plunger, burnt relay contacts, and lost steps.

bank.q: What are fluid-mechanical actuators? Explain hydraulic and pneumatic actuators, the electrically operated valves that control them, and two vehicle applications with sketches.
outline: Definition and F = Δp A, v = Q ÷ A, P = Δp Q
Hydraulic: stiff, high force; pneumatic: compressible, spring-set position
Valves: switching 2/2 and 3/2, PWM, proportional (current-controlled)
Wastegate diaphragm actuator with numbers
Gearbox clutch piston or ABS modulator
answer: Definition: a fluid-mechanical actuator turns the energy of a pressurised fluid (oil, air or vacuum) into force and movement. The ECU commands it through a solenoid valve that meters the fluid; the pump or the engine supplies the energy.
Relations: force F = Δp × A, piston speed v = Q ÷ A, hydraulic power P = Δp × Q, with Δp in Pa, A in m² and Q in m³/s.

Hydraulic actuators use oil at a few bar (cam phasers, transmissions) up to much higher pressures (brakes). Oil hardly compresses, so they are stiff, hold position under load and give large forces from small areas.

Pneumatic actuators use intake vacuum, boost pressure or compressed air. Air compresses, so they are soft and their position is set by balancing the pressure force against a return spring. They are cheap, clean and light.

answer.text: Valves between the ECU and the fluid:

head: Valve
Action
Example
rows: Actuator to supply or to vent
Gearbox pressure control, cam-phaser oil-control valve

answer.pre:
boost ─┬──────────→ [diaphragm Ø 60 mm | spring 90 N, 15 N/mm] → rod → wastegate flap
       └→ PWM vent valve (ECU)

answer: The ECU raises the boost limit by venting part of the actuator pressure through the PWM valve, so the diaphragm sees less than the full boost.

answer.pre: pump → proportional pressure valve (ECU current) → annular piston (D 120 mm, d 80 mm) → clutch pack

A = π (0.120² − 0.080²) ÷ 4 = 6.283 × 10⁻³ m²
at 10 bar: F = 1.0 × 10⁶ × 6.283 × 10⁻³ = 6283 N
fill: 2 mm stroke = 12.6 cm³; at 0.5 L/s it takes 25 ms

answer: The ECU shapes a fill-then-clamp pressure ramp for a smooth shift, and uses current control so coil warming does not change the pressure. Check: a 1 A solenoid commands 6.3 kN because the valve only meters the flow.
Other applications: the ABS modulator (hold, drop and rise of brake pressure), the cam phaser (oil in vane chambers turns the camshaft relative to its sprocket) and hydraulic power steering.

bank.q: Describe the electrical machines used in vehicles: DC machines, three-phase machines and single-phase AC machines. Explain duty-type ratings with examples.
outline: DC machine parts, back emf, V = E + I R<sub>a</sub>, T = kΦ I
PM, series, shunt, compound, brushless; vehicle uses
Three-phase: rotating field, n<sub>s</sub> = 120 f ÷ p; synchronous (alternator, PMSM) and induction
Single-phase: pulsating field, needs starting aid
Duty types S1–S10, CDF, vehicle examples
answer: DC machine construction: a stator field (permanent magnets or a field winding), a rotating armature with coils, and a commutator with brushes that reverses each coil's current as it passes the poles so the torque stays in one direction.

answer.pre:
back emf      E = kΦ ω
voltage       V = E + I R<sub>a</sub>
torque        T = kΦ I
speed         ω = (V − I R<sub>a</sub>) ÷ kΦ

answer.text: Worked line (12 V, R<sub>a</sub> = 0.2 Ω, kΦ = 0.02 V·s/rad):

answer: Three-phase machines: three stator windings 120° apart, fed with three-phase current, make a field rotating at n<sub>s</sub> = 120 f ÷ p. A synchronous machine's rotor (magnets or DC field) turns exactly at n<sub>s</sub>: the claw-pole alternator (three-phase output rectified by a diode bridge) and the PMSM traction motor; 8 poles at 400 Hz gives 6000 rpm. An induction machine's shorted rotor runs at n<sub>s</sub>(1 − s): 4 poles at 200 Hz with 3 % slip gives 5820 rpm. Traction machines take variable-frequency current from an inverter.

Single-phase AC machines: one winding makes a pulsating, not rotating, field, so induction types need a starting aid (a capacitor-fed auxiliary winding or a shaded pole); universal motors run on AC or DC with a commutator. In vehicles they appear only behind an inverter or in workshop and charging equipment.

Duty types (IEC 60034-1): heat limits a motor, and a rating is valid only for its pattern of use. S1 continuous (to thermal equilibrium): radiator fan, fuel pump. S2 short-time (stated minutes, then rest until cold): seat adjuster, sunroof; the starter is an extreme short-time duty. S3 intermittent periodic with a cyclic duration factor: window lift, door lock. S4 and S5 add starting and braking heat; S6 to S10 are continuous running with load or speed changes, such as a traction motor over a drive cycle.
Cyclic duration factor: CDF = t<sub>on</sub> ÷ (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>). A window lift running 4 s and resting 12 s has CDF = 4 ÷ 16 = 25 %, duty S3 25 %.
Consequence: an S2 30 min fan motor fitted where the fan runs for hours in traffic overheats; the duty must match the use.

bank.q: Describe current and voltage measurement in a battery management system and explain how state of charge, state of health and state of function are estimated.
outline: Current: shunt resistor with differential amplifier, or Hall or fluxgate clamp for isolation
Voltage: resistive divider into ADC, per cell and pack level, isolation barrier
Coulomb counting: charge = integral of current over time
SOC from coulomb counting with a model correction at rest, and open-circuit voltage lookup
SOH from capacity fade and internal resistance rise
SOF from available power at present SOC and temperature
answer: Current measurement, shunt: a low resistance (for example 0.1 mΩ) in the pack line; V = I R gives 10 mV at 100 A. Kelvin (four-terminal) connections take the voltage from the resistor body so lead resistance does not add; an amplifier raises it for the ADC, and the shunt's temperature is measured to correct its resistance.

Current measurement, Hall or fluxgate: a core around the conductor concentrates the field of the current onto a Hall element; it gives galvanic isolation and no insertion loss but has more offset and is less accurate at small currents. The sign must be kept: discharge one way, charging and regeneration the other.

Voltage measurement: each cell or module voltage is read by a cell-monitor chip; the pack voltage is scaled by a high-value resistor divider V<sub>adc</sub> = V<sub>pack</sub> R<sub>2</sub> ÷ (R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>) and passed through an isolated amplifier or isolated ADC, so the low-voltage electronics are separated from the high-voltage pack. A 12-bit ADC on 5 V resolves 5 ÷ 4095 = 1.22 mV.
Temperature: NTC thermistors on modules feed the BMS, which limits current when a cell is hot or cold.

answer.pre:
SOC(t) = SOC(0) − (1 ÷ C<sub>n</sub>) ∫ I dt     (I > 0 for discharge, t in hours)
example: 50 Ah at 80 %, 10 A for 0.5 h → 5 Ah removed → 80 % − 5 ÷ 50 = 70 %

answer: Correction: coulomb counting drifts because a current offset or gain error is integrated; after a rest the open-circuit voltage gives SOC from the OCV curve, best near full and empty because the curve is flat in the middle. Production BMSs blend both in a model-based filter.

SOH: compares the present capacity (learnt between two OCV resets from the charge counted) and the internal resistance (ΔV ÷ ΔI at a current step) with the new values; for example 45 Ah of an original 50 Ah is 90 % capacity SOH.

SOF: the power the pack can deliver or accept now, from SOC, temperature and SOH (resistance): a cold, aged or nearly empty pack gives less. The vehicle uses it to decide whether stop-start, boost or regeneration is allowed.
Summary: current, voltage and temperature sensing are the inputs; SOC, SOH and SOF are estimates the BMS computes from them.

bank.q: A crankshaft target wheel has 36 teeth with one tooth missing and runs at 3000 rev/min. Calculate the pulses per revolution, the crank angle per tooth pitch, the tooth-pitch frequency, the time between normal pulses and the length of the gap. Explain how the missing tooth is detected as the reference.
outline: Pulses per revolution = 35
Crank angle per pitch = 360 ÷ 36 = 10°
Pitch frequency = 36 × 50 = 1800 Hz; average pulse rate 35 × 50 = 1750 per second
Normal period T = 1 ÷ 1800 = 0.556 ms
Gap = 2T = 1.111 ms; detected when an interval is about twice the one before
Reference angle stored as calibration before TDC
answer: Data: 36 pitches per revolution, 35 teeth present, n = 3000 rpm = 50 rev/s, so one revolution lasts 1 ÷ 50 = 20 ms.
Pulses per revolution: 35 (one per present tooth).
Crank angle per tooth pitch: 360° ÷ 36 = 10°. Use the pitch count, not the 35 teeth present.
Tooth-pitch frequency: 36 × 50 = 1800 Hz. The average pulse rate is 35 × 50 = 1750 pulses per second, but the spacing is not uniform, so timing uses the pitch.
Time between normal pulses: T = 1 ÷ 1800 = 0.556 ms (= 20 ms ÷ 36).
Gap: from the last tooth before the missing one to the first tooth after it is two pitches, 2T = 1.111 ms.

answer.text: Check that one revolution adds up:
answer.pre:
34 normal intervals × 0.5556 ms = 18.889 ms
 1 gap interval   × 1.1111 ms =  1.111 ms
 total                         = 20.000 ms = 1 ÷ 50 rev/s

answer: Detection: the ECU time-stamps each edge with a capture timer and divides the latest interval by the previous one. Normal intervals give a ratio near 1; the gap gives about 2 (a 60-2 wheel gives 3). A threshold such as 1.5, with a check that the next interval falls back to about 0.5 of the gap, marks the reference and rejects a single noisy edge.

Use of the reference: at the first tooth after the gap the tooth counter is reset and given a calibrated angle (for example 90° before TDC of cylinder 1; the value differs between engines). Angles in between are found by counting teeth of 10° and interpolating in time with the latest T.
During sharp acceleration the gap ratio drifts from exactly 2, which is why the threshold sits well between 1 and 2.

answer.text: The same wheel at other speeds (T = 1 ÷ (36 n)):

answer: At cranking the period itself changes a lot between compression strokes, so the ECU also accepts the gap only near the expected tooth count since the last gap.

bank.q: An NTC coolant sensor forms a voltage divider with a 2.2 kΩ pull-up to a 5 V reference and feeds a 10-bit ADC. For a sensor resistance of 2.2 kΩ, find the divider voltage and the ADC count. The same sensor (B = 3500 K) reads 269 Ω at 90 °C: find the voltage and count there, and state the practical problems of this arrangement.
outline: V<sub>out</sub> = 5 × R<sub>t</sub> ÷ (R<sub>t</sub> + R<sub>pull</sub>) = 2.5 V
Count = round(2.5 × 1023 ÷ 5) = 512; one count 4.89 mV
At 90 °C: 0.545 V, count 111
Non-linear: lookup table
Low resolution when hot; self-heating; wire and ground resistance
answer: Circuit: 5 V reference → 2.2 kΩ pull-up → ECU input node → NTC → sensor ground. The ADC reads the node voltage.
ADC count: round(2.500 × 1023 ÷ 5) = round(511.5) = 512; one count is 5 ÷ 1023 = 4.89 mV.
Problem 1, non-linearity: the voltage is not a straight line in temperature, so the ECU must use a table or the Steinhart–Hart equation; a straight line through two points is wrong in between.

Problem 2, resolution when hot: near 90 °C the curve is flat; between 85 °C and 95 °C the voltage changes by only about 0.13 V (about 26 counts), so one count is worth about 0.4 °C. Many ECUs switch in a smaller second pull-up when warm to spread the hot range.
Problem 3, self-heating: at 25 °C the thermistor carries 5 ÷ 4400 = 1.14 mA and dissipates 1.14 mA² × 2200 ≈ 2.8 mW, which can warm a small bead and make it read high; a larger pull-up lowers this.

Problem 4, wiring: series resistance from a corroded connector or a poor sensor ground adds to the NTC. 100 Ω extra is small against 10 kΩ when cold but large against 269 Ω when hot, so the ECU reads too cold only when the engine is warm.
The ADC reference and the pull-up share the 5 V supply, so slow drift of the 5 V cancels (ratiometric reading).

Remedies: use a second, smaller pull-up (switched in by the ECU above about 50 °C) to spread the hot range, keep the pull-up large enough to limit self-heating, filter the input with an RC low-pass, and run a separate sensor ground wire back to the ECU.

bank.q: A 12 V permanent-magnet radiator-fan motor has R<sub>a</sub> = 0.25 Ω and kΦ = 0.025 V·s/rad. Ignoring friction, find the no-load speed, the speed, torque, output power and efficiency at 8 A, and the stall current and torque. The fan then runs 5 min on and 5 min off in a 10 min cycle: find the cyclic duration factor and state which duty rating the motor needs, and whether an S2 10 min motor would do for traffic driving.
outline: No load: ω = 12 ÷ 0.025 = 480 rad/s (4584 rpm)
Stall: 48 A, 1.20 N·m
Traffic: continuous, needs S1
answer: Equations: E = kΦω, V = E + I R<sub>a</sub>, T = kΦ I, P<sub>out</sub> = T ω.
Output power: 0.20 × 400 = 80 W; input power: 12 × 8 = 96 W; efficiency 80 ÷ 96 = 83.3 %; the 16 W difference is the copper loss 8² × 0.25.
Check: maximum output comes at half the stall torque and half the no-load speed: 0.60 × 240 = 144 W.
Duty: CDF = 5 ÷ (5 + 5) × 100 % = 50 %; identical on–off cycles with little starting heat, so S3 50 % (the 10 min cycle is the standard S3 period).

Traffic: at idle in heavy traffic the fan runs without a break for an hour or more, which is S1 continuous duty. An S2 10 min motor reaches its temperature limit after 10 minutes and keeps heating: its insulation and brushes age, and a thermal cut-out may trip and let the engine overheat. Specify S1 at 80 W, or a larger motor whose continuous rating covers 80 W.
Speed control: the ECU sets fan speed by PWM on a MOSFET; at 50 % duty the mean voltage is 6 V and the no-load speed halves to 240 rad/s.

Losses in the drive: the MOSFET that switches the fan sees 8 A; with R<sub>DS(on)</sub> = 10 mΩ it loses 8² × 0.010 = 0.64 W, small against the 96 W input, so electronic speed control costs little efficiency.

bank.q: State the Hall effect. Compare Hall-effect, variable reluctance and optical sensors for crankshaft position sensing in a hot, oily engine bay; analyse their failure modes and explain how the ECU can limp home when the signal is lost.
outline: Hall effect: V<sub>H</sub> = I B ÷ (n q t)
VR: passive, amplitude grows with speed, none at zero
Hall: needs supply, works at zero speed, clean square wave
Optical: fine resolution but oil and dirt block the light
Failure modes and limp home
Failure modes: open coil, shorted turns, air-gap change, metal debris on the magnet, connector corrosion
Limp home: substitute cam sensor signal, or fixed timing and speed-density fuel, or default to a fixed advance
answer: Hall effect: a current I through a thin semiconductor plate in a field B at right angles pushes the carriers sideways (force q v × B) until a transverse voltage balances it: V<sub>H</sub> = I B ÷ (n q t). With 10 mA, 0.1 T, n = 10²² m⁻³ and t = 0.5 mm: V<sub>H</sub> = 0.010 × 0.1 ÷ (10²² × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 0.0005) = 1.25 mV, so an amplifier and Schmitt trigger follow on the same chip.

head: Feature
Variable reluctance
Hall
Optical
rows: Tolerant (metal debris on magnet is a risk)

answer: Analysis: in a hot, oily engine bay the optical sensor is the weak choice; VR is robust but weak at cranking speed (at 150 rpm a 60-2 wheel gives only 150 Hz and a small amplitude); Hall gives a clean edge from zero speed, which suits quick starts and stop-start engines. Most modern engines therefore use Hall or magnetoresistive crank sensors.

Failure modes: VR: open coil, shorted turns, air gap too large, metal debris on the magnet, a cracked wheel. Hall: lost supply or ground, connector corrosion, IC over-temperature. Optical: dirty lens or disc, LED ageing. All: chafed wires picking up ignition noise, giving false teeth.
Detection: the ECU checks that the tooth count between gaps is right (58 on a 60-2 wheel), that the period changes plausibly, and that crank and cam signals agree.

Limp home: if the crank signal is lost but the cam signal is good, some ECUs run from the cam sensor with fixed, safe advance and less precise timing; if the cam signal is lost, the ECU keeps the crank signal and uses wasted spark and batch injection; with neither the engine stops. A fault code is stored and the warning lamp lit.

Diagnosis: check supply and ground with a meter, then look at the signal on an oscilloscope while cranking: a VR trace should grow with speed and show the gap; a Hall trace should switch cleanly between its two levels.
Judgement: for this engine bay, a Hall (or magnetoresistive) sensor with a VR or cam back-up strategy gives the best start reliability.

bank.q: Evaluate the choice between a narrowband and a wideband oxygen sensor for a petrol engine that must meet close-coupled catalyst light-off and lean-burn operation. Support your answer with the control strategy each sensor allows.
outline: Narrowband: cheap, sharp switch at lambda = 1, only useful for holding stoichiometric
Cannot measure individual cylinder or lean-burn deviation with accuracy
Wideband: pump cell, current proportional to lambda, range roughly lambda 0.7 to air
Enables catalyst heating strategy, individual cylinder trim, lean-burn and ethanol blend adaptation
Needs heater control and a reference air supply, higher cost
Evaluate: emissions benefit and fuel saving against cost and durability of the pump cell
answer: Requirements: fast catalyst light-off after a cold start (the catalyst does nothing until hot) and lean-burn operation at part load for fuel economy. The question is which sensor lets the ECU control both.

Narrowband: a single Nernst cell; about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich, switching only at λ = 1. It is cheap and durable and is ideal for holding λ = 1 with a limit-cycle trim. It cannot say how lean a mixture is: at λ = 1.3 and at λ = 1.05 it reads the same 0.1 V.

Wideband: a pump cell holds a Nernst cell at about 450 mV; the pump current is proportional to oxygen excess or deficit, giving λ from about 0.7 to free air. It needs its own controller and heater control and costs more.

head: Strategy
Narrowband
Wideband
rows: Yes, with a steady λ target
Yes, λ known from early on

answer: Light-off: both need a heater; a planar wideband reaches operating temperature in seconds, so closed loop starts sooner and the ECU can hold a precise slightly lean mixture with retarded spark to heat the catalyst.

Lean burn: only a wideband can hold λ = 1.4 accurately; a narrowband would see a constant "lean" and have no feedback. A NO<sub>x</sub> storage catalyst for lean burn also needs a downstream sensor to judge its purge.
Numbers: at λ = 1.048 (AFR 15.4) a narrowband reads about 0.1 V, the same as at λ = 1.3; a wideband reports 1.048, so the ECU can correct a 4.8 % lean error at once.

Cost and durability: a wideband costs more and its pump cell must be calibrated; the narrowband is simpler. Many engines use a wideband before the catalyst and a narrowband after it as the catalyst monitor.

Evaluation: for close-coupled light-off plus lean burn the wideband upstream sensor is required; its higher cost is repaid by fuel saving and by meeting emission limits, while a cheap narrowband stays downstream for monitoring.

glossary.def: A device that turns an electrical command from the ECU into mechanical movement or flow.
The smallest change in input that the sensor and ADC can distinguish, set by bit count and reference voltage.
The change in output for a unit change in input, for example millivolts per kilopascal for a MAP sensor.
The difference in output when the same input is reached from increasing and from decreasing direction.
Pressure measured with vacuum as the zero reference, so it never goes negative.
Four resistances in a diamond, excited by a supply, giving a near-zero output at balance and a small differential voltage when one arm changes.
A semiconductor resistor whose resistance changes strongly with temperature; NTC types fall in resistance as temperature rises.
Two dissimilar metals joined at a hot junction, producing a small voltage proportional to the temperature difference between junctions.
The ratio of actual air-fuel ratio to the stoichiometric ratio; lambda = 1 means chemically correct.
The percentage correction the ECU applies to injection quantity from oxygen sensor feedback; short term is fast, long term is learned.
Abnormal rapid burning of the end gas in the cylinder, producing a pressure spike and high-frequency block vibration.
Exhaust gas recirculation valve; a solenoid or stepper or vacuum-operated valve that admits exhaust into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx.
An electromagnetic valve that opens for a commanded time to spray a measured fuel quantity.
An electromagnetically operated switch that lets a small ECU current control a large load current.
A diode across an inductive load that gives the collapsing coil current a path, protecting the driving switch.
Battery management system; the electronics that measures cell voltage, current and temperature and estimates SOC, SOH and SOF.
Remaining charge in a battery as a percentage of its rated capacity.
The present capacity and internal resistance of an aged battery compared with its new condition.
The power the battery can actually deliver or accept now, at the present charge and temperature.
An angular-rate sensor, usually vibrating MEMS, whose output voltage is proportional to rotation rate about an axis.
Light detection and ranging; a pulsed laser and detector that measures distance to objects from time of flight, used in driver assistance.
A processor with flash, RAM, EEPROM, ADC, timers and communication on one chip; the heart of every ECU.
A voltage-controlled transistor switch; when on it behaves as a small resistance R<sub>DS(on)</sub>.
A timer that resets the microcontroller if the program stops refreshing it.
A solenoid valve whose spool position or output pressure follows the coil current smoothly.
The voltage a turning motor generates against its supply, E = kΦω.
The load-against-time pattern (S1 to S10) for which a motor rating is valid.
On-time as a percentage of the cycle in an intermittent duty, t<sub>on</sub> ÷ (t<sub>on</sub> + t<sub>off</sub>).
Speed of the rotating field of a three-phase machine, 120 f ÷ p in rpm.
A pneumatic actuator in which pressure on a diaphragm works against a return spring.
